subject: Calculation of linear predictors in a random slope model

messages.author: 3f37be0cf708d442
messages.subject: Calculation of linear predictors in a random slope model
parts:
Hello,

I'd like to calculate linear predictors that are generated by inla.posterior.sample myself from a design matrix and sampled parameters. (to ultimately compute average marginal effects). 

However, when i compare the linear predictors from inla.posterior.sample with the ones i calculated myself, i find that they are not identical, but correlated with (only)  r=.75. Haakon's post https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic112.html#64_alternative_way:_building_up_the_samples_model_component_by_model_component suggests to me that one I should be able to calculate the exact values of the linear predictor.

I would appreciate if somebody could have a look and tell me if there is a mistake in my code below:

# random slope model
f = sumscore ~ supp_5y_YN + supp_5y_HRS + pre + nMHPs__5y +
               f(my_datal$ID, model="iid") +
               f(ngroup, model = "iid3d", n = 3*n_groups) +
               f(ngroup1, supp_5y_YN, copy = "ngroup") +
               f(ngroup2, supp_5y_HRS, copy = "ngroup")

# fit model
inla_fit =
  inla(f,
       data = my_datal,
       family = "betabinomial",
       Ntrials = nT,
       weights = my_datal$sipw,
       control.compute=list(config = TRUE),
       control.predictor=list(compute = TRUE))

# get posterior samples
ps = inla.posterior.sample(250,inla_fit)

# extract one sample
L = ps[[1]]$latent
# extract automatically generated linear predictors
lin_pred_inla = L[grep("Predictor",row.names(L)),]
# extract model parameters by removing linear predictors from L
L = L[-grep("Predictor",row.names(L)),]

# put complete model matrix (random  + fixed effects) X together
X_ID_iid = sapply(unique(my_datal$ID),
                  function(i) my_datal$ID == i)
X_group_intercept = sapply(unique(my_datal$ngroup),
                           function(g) (my_datal$ngroup == g)*1)
X_group_supp_5y_YN = sapply(unique(my_datal$ngroup),
                            function(g) (my_datal$ngroup == g)*my_datal$supp_5y_YN)
X_group_supp_5y_HRS = sapply(unique(my_datal$ngroup),
                            function(g) (my_datal$ngroup == g)*my_datal$supp_5y_HRS)
X_fixed_effects = as.matrix(inla_fit$model.matrix)

X = cbind(X_ID_iid,
          X_group_intercept,
          X_group_supp_5y_YN,
          X_group_supp_5y_HRS,
          X_fixed_effects)

# remove duplicate parameters
# not sure if one can just use the first of the 3 (near-) replicates
# but results do not get better if I average over the 3 replicates
pars = L[grep("group1:|group2:",names(L),invert = T)]
pars[grep("group:",names(L))] = rowMeans(matrix(L[grep("group",names(L))],nrow = 18))

# "manually" calculate linear predictors
lin_pred = X %*% pars

plot(lin_pred_inla,lin_pred,
     main = cor(lin_pred_inla,
                lin_pred,
                use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))



One thing that I do fundamentally not understand is what is behind the 3 near-replicates of the three correlated random effects. Why are those near-identical and not completely identical?

Thanks in advance!
Guido

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Calculation of linear predictors in a random slope model
parts:
I would suggest to look at the function

inla.posterior.sample.eval

and example, which will simplify life....

One thing that I do fundamentally not understand is what is behind
> the 3 near-replicates of the three correlated random effects. Why are
> those near-identical and not completely identical?

the 'copy' model, says that a copy, X2, of X1, is constructed so that

X2 = Normal(X1, small.noise)

and this small noise is required so that the joint model is not singular.

The details are spelled out here

@Article{art522,
author = {T. G. Martins and D. Simpson and F. Lindgren and H. Rue},
title = {Bayesian computing with {INLA}: {N}ew features},
journal = CSDA,
keywords = {year2013,my.own,my.cv},
year = 2013,
volume = 67,
pages = {68--83}
}



H

Thanks for the explanation of the random effects parameters.

For others' who might read this:  "inla.posterior.sample.eval" is not part of current stable release (INLA_18.07.12), but can be found in the current testing version (INLA_19.05.19).

I looked at inla.posterior.sample.eval and understand what it does. But my key question remains:
Why can't i recover the linear predictor with the following code?
[recovering the linear predictor is only a test, which I want to be sure to get right, before I calculate average marginal effects].

So here is the modified code with which I am trying to recover the linear predictors:

### fit model in INLA ###

f = sumscore ~ supp_5y_YN + supp_5y_HRS +
               pre + nMHPs__5y +
               f(my_datal$ID, model="iid") +
               f(ngroup, model = "iid3d", n = 3*n_groups) +
               f(ngroup1, supp_5y_YN, copy = "ngroup") +
               f(ngroup2, supp_5y_HRS, copy = "ngroup")

inla_fit =
  inla(f,

data = my_datal,
       family = "betabinomial",
       Ntrials = nT,
       weights = my_datal$sipw,
       control.compute=list(config = TRUE),
       control.predictor=list(compute = TRUE))

## generate sample and extract linear predictors
ps = inla.posterior.sample(100,inla_fit)
lin_pred_inla = L[grep("Predictor",row.names(L)),]

## prepare design matrix for "manual" calculation of linear predictors
ngroup = my_datal$ngroup
X_ID_iid = sapply(unique(my_datal$ID),
                  function(i) my_datal$ID == i)
X_group_intercept = sapply(unique(ngroup),
                           function(g) (ngroup == g)*1)
X_group_supp_5y_YN = sapply(unique(ngroup),
                            function(g) (ngroup == g)*my_datal$supp_5y_YN)
X_group_supp_5y_HRS = sapply(unique(ngroup),
                            function(g) (ngroup == g)*my_datal$supp_5y_HRS)

X_fixed_effects = as.matrix(inla_fit$model.matrix)

X = cbind(X_ID_iid,
          X_group_intercept,
          X_group_supp_5y_YN,
          X_group_supp_5y_HRS,
          X_fixed_effects)

## get parameters across all samples
get_pars = function() {
  return(c(`my_datal|S|ID`,
           ngroup,
           Intercept, supp_5y_YN, supp_5y_HRS, pre, nMHPs__5y))
}
pars = inla.posterior.sample.eval(get_pars,ps)

## manually calculate linear predictors
lin_pred_manual = rowMeans(X %*% pars)


when i do this, lin_pred_inla and lin_pred_manual are highly correlated (r > .8) , but I think they should be identical.

Now I am wondering for example if the way i put the design martrix random effects together is wrong, but I don't see where this should be. (I couldn't find an inla-function to access the random effects design matrix used by inla)

Best, Guido

parts:
I figured out that the problem was an error in my code,

I had compared the linear predictor of one sample with the the average of linear predictors across all samples. Because of copy-pasting errors, the last code snippet I had was unclear beyond the error. here is the working code:

# define and fit model

f = sumscore ~ supp_5y_YN + supp_5y_HRS +
  pre + nMHPs__5y +
  f(my_datal$ID, model="iid") +
  f(ngroup, model = "iid3d", n = 3*n_groups) +
  f(ngroup1, supp_5y_YN, copy = "ngroup") +
  f(ngroup2, supp_5y_HRS, copy = "ngroup")

inla_fit =
  inla(f,

data = my_datal,
       family = "betabinomial",
       Ntrials = nT,
       weights = my_datal$sipw,
       control.compute=list(config = TRUE),
       control.predictor=list(compute = TRUE))

ps = inla.posterior.sample(100,inla_fit)

## put design matrix together
## put design matrix together
group_re = model.matrix(~0 + factor(ngroup),my_datal)
support_YN =  my_datal$supp_5y_YN
support_HRS = my_datal$supp_5y_HRS
X = 
  cbind(model.matrix(~0 + factor(ID),my_datal),  # individ. random intercepts
        group_re,                                # group random intercept
        apply(group_re, 2,
              function(x) x * support_YN),       # group random slope 1
        apply(group_re,2,                        # group random slope 2
              function(x) x * support_HRS),
        as.matrix(inla_fit$model.matrix)         # fixed effects
  )

## extract parameters from posterior samples

get_pars = function() {
  return(c(`my_datal|S|ID`,
           ngroup,
           Intercept, supp_5y_YN, supp_5y_HRS, pre, nMHPs__5y))
}

get_linpred = function() {
  return(c(Predictor))
}

## regression parameters
pars = inla.posterior.sample.eval(get_pars,ps)
lin_pred = rowMeans(X %*% pars)

## linear predictors from INLA
lin_pred_inla = rowMeans(inla.posterior.sample.eval(get_linpred,ps))
